newsitem.title: USA: Helicopter sent to suspected warplane crash site.
newsitem.headline: Helicopter sent to suspected warplane crash site.

text.p: A search and rescue helicopter was dispatched on Wednesday to a snowy peak in the Rocky Mountains where wreckage of a warplane that disappeared three weeks ago is believed buried, an Air Force official said.
"They will try to retrieve a piece or pieces of metal. That is their mission," Capt. Mike Richmond said by telephone from Eagle, Colorado.

He said the search and rescue team aboard the helicopter would be lowered on ropes to the crash site where they would attach cables to pieces of wreckage so it could be flown back to Eagle for examination.

He said clearing skies allowed the MH-53 heavy lift helicopter, the strongest and most powerful helicopter the Air Force has, to take off for the site where the A-10 Thunderbolt attack bomber is thought to have slammed into the side of the 12,500-foot (3,800-metre) -high New York Mountain in the remote Sawatch range southeast of the Vail ski resort.
He said two A-10 pilots were on hand at the rescue headquarters in Eagle to examine the pieces of wreckage.
"They are familiar with the aircraft and should be able to say whether or not these pieces came from an A-10," he adeed.
The wreckage of a plane that officials said was "likely" the missing aircraft was spotted on Sunday by an Army National Guard helicopter crew near a steep cliff on New York Mountain.
The A-10 Thunderbolt disappeared during a routine training mission on April 2.

Air Force officials have been at a loss to explain why the pilot, Capt. Craig Button, 32, left the three-plane delta formation in which it was flying and apparently veered northeast into Colorado, some 850 miles (1,350 km) away from the training exercise.

Button, whose plane was carrying four 500-pound (225-kg) Mark 82 conventional bombs, broke formation after leaving the Davis-Monthan Air Force Base near Tucson, Arizona, en route for the Barry M. Goldwater Bombing Range in Arizona.
